title: Laowa's New 24mm f/2 Tilt-Shift Beats Canon's TS-E 24mm on Medium Format
summary: Laowa launches new 24mm f/2 tilt-shift lens designed to outperform Canon on medium format
detailed: Shift lenses keep a building's verticals straight while the camera stays level, and they do it without the unpredictable cropping and resolution loss you take on when you fix perspective in software.
Laowa's new 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift brings that to most mirrorless mounts and to medium format, at an aperture tilt-shift lenses almost never reach.
Keith Cooper has shot with a Canon TS-E 24mm f/3.5L II for years, so he knows where to look.
On the GFX, the 24mm gives you a view close to a 19mm lens on full frame, and Cooper found he could use the full range of shift without significant problems.
sentences: Shift lenses keep a building's verticals straight while the camera stays level, and they do it without the unpredictable cropping and resolution loss you take on when you fix perspective in software.
Laowa's new 24mm f/2 Zero-D Tilt-Shift brings that to most mirrorless mounts and to medium format, at an aperture tilt-shift lenses almost never reach.
Keith Cooper has shot with a Canon TS-E 24mm f/3.5L II for years, so he knows where to look.
After adapting it to a Fujifilm GFX100S and comparing it with the Laowa, on loan from the company, he finds the newer lens clearly ahead in flare control and in corner quality.
The gap narrows on a smaller full frame sensor, but it doesn't close.
On the GFX, the 24mm gives you a view close to a 19mm lens on full frame, and Cooper found he could use the full range of shift without significant problems.
Laowa lists the image circle at 67 mm, though his results suggest it runs slightly larger.
If you shoot medium format, you've had very few shift options that hold up at the edges, and this widens that short list.
Most of his sample frames came from a walk through a city center on the way to an event, and nearly all of them were shot handheld.
Cooper is blunt about the old rule that these lenses demand a tripod.
You need a steady shutter speed and a level camera, and practice handles the rest.
He also uses diagonal shift often, and his storefront examples show how a small diagonal move can bring in street context that a straight vertical shift leaves out.
For most work, he shoots it at f/8 or f/11, and he goes to f/11 when he's using a lot of shift and the corners hold important detail.
Take the petal hood off when you shift a lot, or it will cause hard vignetting at the edges of the frame.
The lens is fully manual and sends nothing to the camera.
As far as the body is concerned, no lens is attached, so you get no aperture, tilt, or shift data in the EXIF, and lens correction profiles won't apply.
Keep a notebook if those details matter later.
You can still fine-tune perspective in Lightroom, Photoshop, or DxO software, and Cooper does, but he gets the framing close in camera first.
Mirrorless mounts have quietly opened the door for lenses like this one.
The short flange distance gives designers room to build a lens that shifts across a large image circle without bulking up the way older DSLR designs did.
Laowa skipped Canon EF entirely for that reason.
Medium format shooters on Fujifilm long relied on the Fujifilm GF30mmF5.6 T/S and GF110mmF5.6 T/S Macro, or on adapted full frame glass that often showed mount vignetting once shifted.
This Laowa shows none that Cooper can detect, which points to a design aimed at larger sensors from the start.
Newer optical glass and far better lens design software also give a current lens a head start over one designed well over a decade ago.

Wherever you shoot, the takeaway holds: correct as much as you can with the lens, and leave post-processing for small adjustments, because every degree of software correction costs you pixels and makes the final crop harder to predict.
At f/2, tilt becomes far easier to see.
Cooper's examples at a café table run a thin plane of focus through a cup of coffee, leaving part of a spoon sharp and the rest soft.
Tilt can also swing that thin plane to different angles, depending on where the tilt axis sits, and it handles the miniature-world look too.
The GF30mm, at f/5.6, can't produce that razor-thin look.
He also warns about the new-toy effect: an image that excites you today may look forced a week from now.
Mechanically, the tilt has no detent or lock at zero.
After one trip in his camera bag, a slight leftover tilt left one side of his frames softer than the other.
If you plan to stitch panoramas with left and right shift, Cooper's light box tests in the video show the vignetting dropping off sharply once you stop down past about f/4, even at full shift.
